title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
authors: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

infographic.key_insight: For shape-informed hemodynamic surrogates, active learning and finite-element physical consistency constraints are more effective during fine-tuning than early training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework advances scalable, patient-specific prediction of aortic velocity and pressure fields toward real-time cardiovascular assessment.
method: Generate physiologically consistent CFD data from SynthAorta geometries using automatic boundary-condition adjustment.
Represent anatomies as displacement fields on a common reference geometry and train Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogates.
Fine-tune using active learning and differentiable finite-element residual constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Peak-systolic evaluations report fine-tuning gains from gradient- and subspace-based acquisition, while out-of-distribution tests identify geometric parametrization support as the main limitation.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization remains constrained by the anatomical variability covered by the geometric parametrization; changing network architecture alone may not resolve this.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics

title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers
authors: Zumrat Usmanova, Ruobing Bai
abstract: A liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) exhibits a two-way coupling between its mesogen order and network elasticity: the mesogen order sets the undeformed network conformation, and the network deformation reorients the mesogens. This coupling gives rise to large, reversible stimuli-responsive actuation, as well as to soft elasticity, a finite deformation at nearly zero stress. This article reviews the elastic theory of ideal LCEs, bridging single-chain statistics and continuum constitutive models. The "ideal" elastic behavior rests on the assumption of anisotropic Gaussian chains that retain no memory of the crosslinking state, such that rotating the director costs no free energy. The corresponding neo-classical free energy of a monodomain LCE is non-quasi-convex, with a continuous family of stress-free ground states, leading to thermally induced spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity accommodated by coexisting stripe domains. The quasi-convex relaxation of the free energy classifies the behavior of polydomain LCEs into three phases, each with a distinct macroscopic mechanical response depending on the stretch state. The ideal elastic theory can be further extended to incorporate additional behaviors and physical processes, including thermo- and photomechanical coupling, Frank elasticity from director distortion, semi-soft or non-soft behavior arising from network nonideality, and temperature- and rate-dependent viscoelasticity.

infographic.key_insight: Ideal liquid crystal elastomers couple mesogen orientation with network deformation, enabling reversible actuation and finite soft deformation at nearly zero stress.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory provides a constitutive foundation for modeling compliant actuators and adaptive structures made from liquid crystal elastomers.
method: Review anisotropic Gaussian-chain statistics and the neo-classical continuum free energy.
Connect stress-free ground states to spontaneous deformation and soft stripe-domain formation.
Use quasi-convex energy relaxation to classify polydomain responses into three stretch-dependent phases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a theoretical review and three-phase classification, but reports no experimental datasets or quantitative validation.
infographic.watch_item: The ideal model assumes no memory of the crosslinking state; realistic predictions may require nonideality, director-gradient, and viscoelastic extensions.
infographic.paper_title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers

title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?
authors: Pratik Worah, Randall Bateman
abstract: Progressive neuronal loss is the hallmark of neurodegenerative disease, yet how loss of neurons shapes the pattern of cognitive decline remains poorly understood. Here we systematically ablate neurons (computational units) in language models spanning recurrent long short-term memory (LSTM) and Transformer architectures and apply limited fine-tuning as a simple proxy for compensatory plasticity. With whole-unit ablation, LSTMs degrade gradually with syntactic and semantic faculties declining in parallel across mild-to-moderate damage. By contrast, Transformers exhibit late threshold-like collapse under feedforward multi-layer perceptron (MLP) ablation and smoother sigmoid-like decline under attention-head ablation. Qualitatively, MLP-ablated models continue to make within-category semantic substitutions (semantic paraphasias) alongside rising non-responses, paralleling Wernicke-type aphasia, while attention-head ablation produces a trend toward loss of semantic specificity similar to the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (svPPA). These findings indicate that feedforward and attentional pathways have functionally distinct failure modes, suggesting that architecture-dependent failure profiles may offer new computational perspectives on aphasic syndromes and neurodegenerative diseases as an in silico model. Notably, early accuracy retention under Transformer attention-head ablation qualitatively parallels pre-symptomatic reserve before the 40--60% neuronal loss reported by Gomez-Isla et al. (1996) when clinical symptoms emerge in Alzheimer's disease, whereas the steadier LSTM decline parallels the symptomatic progression described by DeKosky and Scheff (1990) and Terry et al. (1991).

infographic.key_insight: Neuronal ablation produces architecture-dependent language failures: gradual decline in LSTMs, threshold-like collapse from Transformer MLP damage, and smoother decline from attention-head damage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These failure profiles offer a computational damage-tolerance perspective on language-model robustness, rather than evidence about physical fracture or solid mechanics.
method: Systematically ablate computational units in LSTM and Transformer language models.
Compare Transformer MLP ablation with attention-head ablation.
Apply limited fine-tuning as a proxy for compensatory plasticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parallel syntactic and semantic decline in LSTMs, semantic substitutions and increasing non-responses after MLP ablation, and reduced semantic specificity after attention-head ablation.
infographic.watch_item: Parallels with aphasia and neurodegeneration are qualitative; computational ablation and limited fine-tuning do not establish biological equivalence.
infographic.paper_title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?

title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
authors: Reza T Batley, Sourav Saha
abstract: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. This work presents a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework; a conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are then refined in latent space by exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. The resulting unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints. In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produce printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1\% across six prescribed engineering moduli. Constructing the implant from a single tiled cell reproduces intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1\% and regional strain energy within 0.35\% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. These results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs. The framework is general enough for extending to many other multiscale structural design applications including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.

infographic.key_insight: Rectified-flow generation paired with exact latent-space refinement enables concurrent design of printable bone-scaffold microstructures and their spatial assignments to meet mechanical targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports porous, mechanically matched implants by jointly optimizing scaffold architecture across microstructural and anatomical scales.
method: Generate periodic lattice cells with a conditional rectified-flow model.
Refine cells in latent space using exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities.
Jointly optimize cell geometries and spatial assignments under mechanical and feature-size constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Computational benchmarks report under 1% error across six target moduli for all eight rabbit flow-started refinements, plus human scaffolds with 63% cortical porosity and compliance within 2%, and 84% cancellous porosity with strain-energy deviations below 0.25%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational performance but does not establish fabricated-scaffold validation, manufacturing robustness, or biological outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement

title: Inverse domain uncertainty quantification in hemodynamics: sampling virtual patient cohorts under constraints
authors: Francesco Romor, Jose Rodrigo Rojo-Garcia, André-Alexander Zepernick, Ana Djurdjevac, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: We consider the following inverse domain uncertainty quantification problem: given a prescribed value or measurement of a hemodynamic biomarker, characterize the distribution of vascular geometries compatible with it. The problem is formulated as a Bayesian inverse problem in which a high-dimensional latent parameter encodes the cardiovascular shape and accounts for inter-patient variability. The parameter-to-observable map composes a conditional LDDMM stochastic interpolant generating the aortic surface with a high-performance numerical finite element solver for the unsteady incompressible Navier--Stokes equations, from which biomarkers of interest are evaluated. The map is nonlinear, high-dimensional and computationally expensive. To address the problem, we compare three ensemble strategies: ensemble adjusted Kalman inversion (EAKI), adaptive Bayesian updating with structural reliability (aBUS), and a Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao (WFR) sequential Monte Carlo scheme. The first two approaches are derivative-free. For the third method, we introduce a novel differentiable flow-matching surrogate that reduces the cost of a single forward map evaluation at the price of a distribution shift depending on the training distribution used for the surrogate. We apply the framework to the generation of virtual patient cohorts matching prescribed pressure drops along aortic geometries affected by coarctation, and we validate and compare the three methods on synthetic data.

infographic.key_insight: Bayesian inverse modeling generates virtual aortic cohorts compatible with prescribed hemodynamic biomarkers rather than identifying a single geometry.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports uncertainty-aware virtual patient generation for aortic coarctation studies constrained by pressure-drop measurements.
method: Encode vascular shape in a high-dimensional latent space and generate aortic surfaces with a conditional LDDMM stochastic interpolant.
Evaluate biomarkers using finite element simulations of unsteady incompressible Navier–Stokes flow.
Compare EAKI, aBUS, and WFR sequential Monte Carlo, introducing a differentiable flow-matching surrogate for the WFR approach.
infographic.evidence_signal: The three strategies are validated and compared on synthetic data for cohorts matching prescribed pressure drops in coarcted aortas.
infographic.watch_item: The surrogate reduces forward-evaluation cost but introduces distribution shift that depends on its training distribution.
infographic.paper_title: Inverse domain uncertainty quantification in hemodynamics: sampling virtual patient cohorts under constraints

title: CAST: Cast-Admissible Generative Design and Shape Optimization with Paired Depth Images
authors: Jihoon Kim, Yongmin Kwon, Namwoo Kang
abstract: Deep generative design can produce complex geometries, but unconstrained representations may create undercuts that prevent release from a two-part mold. We present CAST, which reformulates three-dimensional shape generation under a selected mold-opening constraint as a two-dimensional image generation problem using paired top and bottom depth images. Each valid depth pair defines one material interval along a selected mold-opening direction, so reconstructions exclude undercuts in that direction by construction. Diffusion models generate candidate shapes in this representation, and a finite element analysis (FEA) guided optimizer refines the same two boundaries. We evaluate diffusion-based generation with limited training data comprising 211 SimJEB bracket designs. On SimJEB brackets, FEA-guided refinement with a volume penalty reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates. The median reduction across all candidates was 36.8 percent in the optimization FEA model. Reconstruction of existing brackets revealed a mass--stiffness trade-off: filling occluded regions increased material volume and reduced displacement under the evaluated loads. Paired depth images thus connect generative exploration and structural refinement in a shared design space that preserves the selected pull-direction restriction.

infographic.key_insight: CAST represents 3D shapes as paired top and bottom depth images, excluding undercuts along a selected mold-opening direction by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared representation connects generative shape exploration with FEA-guided structural refinement while preserving the selected pull-direction restriction.
method: Encode geometry as paired depth images defining one material interval along each pull-direction ray.
Train diffusion models to generate candidate shapes in this representation.
Refine both depth boundaries using FEA-guided optimization with a volume penalty.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 211 SimJEB training designs, refinement reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates, with a 36.8% median reduction across all candidates in the optimization FEA model.
infographic.watch_item: Undercut exclusion applies only to the selected pull direction; reconstructing existing shapes can fill occluded regions and increase material volume.
infographic.paper_title: CAST: Cast-Admissible Generative Design and Shape Optimization with Paired Depth Images

title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning
authors: Yongyi Wu, Zheng Wang, Sen Lin
abstract: Online Continual Learning (OCL) requires models to learn from non-stationary data streams under a strict single-pass constraint, making them highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. While existing studies have explored various strategies from data, architecture, and optimization perspectives, the optimizer often directly uses generic approaches such as SGD and AdamW. In this work, we reveal a new link between optimization dynamics and OCL needs by recasting Polyak-Ruppert averaging as the engine of "plasticity" and Primal averaging as the anchor of "stability". This inspires our novel optimizer, SPIN (Stability-Plasticity INterpolation), which explicitly decouples plasticity and stability by interpolating between a fast-moving "plasticity" sequence and an adaptive "stability" sequence. We theoretically demonstrate that SPIN implicitly employs an inverse Hessian approximation, providing crucial Tikhonov regularization to damp noisy, single-sample Hessian estimates and mitigate forgetting. More importantly, SPIN can be seamlessly integrated into existing OCL methods by taking resulted gradients as input and replacing standard optimizers. Extensive experiments show that using SPIN instead of standard optimizers yields consistent and significant performance gains across multiple OCL approaches, including the challenging rehearsal-free setting and under strict memory constraints.

infographic.key_insight: SPIN targets catastrophic forgetting in online continual learning by interpolating between a fast-moving plasticity sequence and an adaptive stability sequence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SPIN could support models that adapt to evolving engineering data streams, but the abstract does not demonstrate solid mechanics or constitutive modeling applications.
method: Uses Polyak–Ruppert averaging to promote plasticity and primal averaging to anchor stability.
Implicitly approximates an inverse Hessian with Tikhonov regularization to damp noisy curvature estimates.
Replaces standard optimizers while accepting gradients from existing online continual learning methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent performance gains across multiple online continual learning approaches, including rehearsal-free learning and strict memory constraints, without specifying benchmarks or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Validate optimizer settings and stability–plasticity behavior on the target data stream before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning

title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models
authors: Alessandro Palma, Charles Jones, Tristan Cinquin, Fabian J. Theis, Frederik Wenkel
abstract: Adapting pre-trained continuous-time generative models to sequentially incoming data without forgetting earlier tasks is a central challenge in lifelong learning. A leading strategy, generative replay, uses a generative model trained on historical tasks to augment its own continual update with synthetic samples from experience. However, it requires full trajectory simulations at every training step, which accumulate discretization errors and can degrade the replayed historical distribution. Here, we propose trajectory replay, which bypasses sample generation by training an updated velocity field to match both a frozen historical velocity along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field, weighted by a stability-plasticity coefficient. Through the lens of continuous-time transport, we show the resulting optimum averages the two task velocities by their respective densities and generates the mixture of their probability paths. Combined with mean velocity distillation, trajectory replay accesses historical trajectories using only a few network evaluations per continual update. Empirically, it outperforms generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation. In two biological case studies, trajectory replay extends generative perturbation models to new contexts and experimental batches across two data modalities while preserving treatment-effect prediction.

infographic.key_insight: Trajectory replay updates continuous-time generative models while retaining past tasks by learning a density-weighted mixture of historical and incoming velocity fields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support continual updates to generative engineering models, but the abstract provides no solid-mechanics or constitutive-model validation.
method: Match frozen historical velocities along their trajectories and incoming-task velocities.
Balance retention and adaptation with a stability–plasticity coefficient.
Use mean velocity distillation to access historical trajectories with few network evaluations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements over generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation, plus preserved treatment-effect prediction in two biological case studies across two data modalities.
infographic.watch_item: Retention depends on the frozen historical model and the stability–plasticity balance; performance on mechanics data remains untested in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models

title: Learning without Overwriting: Structural Knowledge Fusion for Continual Learning
authors: Kanishk Bakshi, Amitansu Pattanaik, Kathiravan Srinivasan
abstract: Catastrophic forgetting in sequential deep learning arises from a fixed-capacity architectural constraint: parameter updates encoding new tasks perturb weight subspaces supporting prior representations. We introduce the Knowledge Fusion Network (KFN), which mitigates the stability-plasticity trade-off in class-incremental learning through novelty-gated structural expansion rather than parameter negotiation within a shared capacity budget. KFN decouples task acquisition from knowledge consolidation: each incoming task is learned in an isolated lightweight specialist network (2.8M parameters) and integrated into the global model via a Structural Fusion Module that allocates dedicated channel capacity conditioned on a quantitative novelty score. Dual structural isolation--channel-space separation with temporally phased gradient unfreezing--protects consolidated knowledge. On ten-task Split CIFAR-100, KFN achieves 11.94% minimum task accuracy and 71.16% task-10 accuracy, whereas shared-parameter baselines degrade severely: LwF to 9.07% average accuracy (0.00% min), Replay++ to 8.91% (85.08% forgetting), and Replay to 16.21% (73.44% forgetting); KFN's forgetting (57.92%) is 15.5 pp lower than Replay. Furthermore, KFN prevents logit-scale drift, maintaining near-symmetric task performance. Across CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT satellite imagery, KFN's class-incremental retention (72.7% and 42.5%) substantially exceeds the best baselines (29.6% and 0.94%). Crucially, KFN achieves parameter-efficient linear scaling, adding 25% of the base parameter count per step and requiring 25.1% of naive backbone duplication over ten tasks (28.1M vs 112.0M). With a 37.1% peak GPU memory reduction over full retraining, KFN establishes novelty-gated expansion as a practical path beyond fixed-capacity architectures.

infographic.key_insight: Knowledge Fusion Network (KFN) reduces catastrophic forgetting by adding novelty-gated channel capacity instead of forcing new tasks into fixed shared parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: KFN could support engineering models that learn sequentially from new datasets, although the abstract does not validate solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling applications.
method: Learn each incoming task in an isolated 2.8M-parameter specialist.
Fuse specialists into the global model using novelty-conditioned channel allocation.
Protect consolidated knowledge through channel separation and phased gradient unfreezing.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Split CIFAR-100 and EuroSAT, KFN reports class-incremental retention of 72.7% and 42.5%, versus best-baseline values of 29.6% and 0.94%; ten-task model size is 28.1M parameters versus 112.0M for naive backbone duplication.
infographic.watch_item: Capacity still grows with tasks, and reported CIFAR-100 forgetting remains substantial at 57.92%.
infographic.paper_title: Learning without Overwriting: Structural Knowledge Fusion for Continual Learning

title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
authors: Xiaoyin Chen, Yizheng Huang, Yinglun Xu, Ziyun Zhao, Emmett McQuinn, Julie Liu
abstract: Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self-modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolving agents remain incomplete continual learners.

infographic.key_insight: Self-evolving agents often improve overall performance, but greater adaptability can undermine retention of earlier knowledge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering assistants adapting to new tools and workflows need regression checks to protect previously reliable capabilities.
method: Keep model weights frozen while adapting prompts, memory, or skills from task feedback.
Compare ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness across drifting task streams.
Assess adaptation, retention, and interference as topics, workflows, or domains shift.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four streams built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld, self-evolution improved aggregate performance on most streams but exposed stability–plasticity trade-offs.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no solid-mechanics-specific validation; global edits and conflicting memory retrieval remain deployment risks.
infographic.paper_title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?

title: A Novel Two-Level Domain Decomposition Method with Physically Motivated Coarse Space for Surface Acoustic Wave Device Simulations
authors: Likun Qiu, Jianguo Huang, Xuejun Xu
abstract: The surface acoustic wave (SAW) equations are fundamental in describing the operating principle of SAW devices, which are characterized by high operating frequency, multiphysics coupling, and defined on an unbounded domain. Finite element (FE) simulation is one of the most accurate numerical methods for such devices. However, the method usually leads to ill-conditioned linear systems with a large number of degrees of freedom (DOFs), limiting its application. To address this issue, based on the finite element tearing and interconnecting (FETI) algorithm, this paper proposes a domain decomposition method with iteration numbers stable with respect to number of subdomains, frequency and mesh size, named FETI-SAW. The main novelty is that the Dirichlet preconditioner combined with a Rayleigh-wave-based coarse space is constructed to produce a preconditioned iterative algorithm for the Lagrange multiplier linear system. In some sense, this method reflects the physical essence of the SAW equations. In numerical experiments, we take interdigital transducers (IDT) and SAW resonators as examples to demonstrate the efficiency of the FETI-SAW algorithm. Additionally, the MATLAB and C++ source codes accompanying this paper are provided.

infographic.key_insight: FETI-SAW combines domain decomposition with a Rayleigh-wave-based coarse space to stabilize iteration counts across subdomain counts, frequencies, and mesh sizes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets large, ill-conditioned finite element systems arising in high-frequency, multiphysics surface acoustic wave device simulations.
method: Partition the finite element problem using finite element tearing and interconnecting (FETI).
Construct a physically motivated coarse space based on Rayleigh waves.
Apply a Dirichlet preconditioner with coarse-space correction to the Lagrange multiplier system.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on interdigital transducers and SAW resonators demonstrate efficiency; accompanying MATLAB and C++ source codes are provided.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract gives no quantitative speedups or setup costs, so practical gains require checking coarse-space construction and solver performance on the target device.
infographic.paper_title: A Novel Two-Level Domain Decomposition Method with Physically Motivated Coarse Space for Surface Acoustic Wave Device Simulations

title: Abaqus implementation of the phase-field approach to fracture
authors: Jiangwei Zhou, Victor Lefevre, Oscar Lopez-Pamies
abstract: In this paper, we introduce an Abaqus user-subroutine implementation of the phase-field model of fracture initiated by Kumar, Francfort, and Lopez-Pamies (\emph{J. Mech. Phys. Solids} 112, 523--551, 2018). The implementation is presented for the basic case of isotropic linear elastic brittle materials with a Drucker-Prager strength surface. The material inputs are therefore the Young's modulus $E$, the Poisson's ratio $ν$, the uniaxial tensile strength $\sts$, the uniaxial compressive strength $\scs$, and the fracture toughness $G_c$. The mathematical correspondence between the heat equation and the evolution equation for the phase field $v(\bfX,t)$ is exploited through a UMAT subroutine, wherein the driving force $c_{\texttt{e}}(\bfX,t)$ --- accounting for the material strength surface --- in the phase-field model plays the role of a heat source. To ensure that the equations for the displacement field $\bfu(\bfX,t)$ and the phase field $v(\bfX,t)$ are solved in a staggered manner --- a solution strategy that, as opposed to monolithic approaches, reliably yields the correct physical solution --- we make use of a combination of UEXTERNALDB, UAMP, MPC, and URDFIL subroutines. Within this approach, the MPC and URDFIL subroutines are additionally utilized to enforce the required bounding and irreversibility inequalities on $v(\bfX,t)$ via a primal-dual active set approach. The capabilities and robustness of the proposed implementation are demonstrated by simulating the ``Nine Circles of Elastic Brittle Fracture'' on a silicate glass --- a set of tests that span the entire range of well-settled experimental knowledge on fracture nucleation and propagation. These simulations also serve to illustrate the deployment of the code using several native Abaqus finite elements, including the simplicial elements CPS3, CAX3, and C3D4.

infographic.key_insight: An Abaqus subroutine implementation combines phase-field fracture with a Drucker–Prager strength surface to model brittle fracture nucleation and propagation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can simulate isotropic linear-elastic brittle materials using elastic moduli, tensile and compressive strengths, and fracture toughness as material inputs.
method: Exploit the heat-equation analogy in UMAT, treating the strength-dependent phase-field driving force as a heat source.
Coordinate UEXTERNALDB, UAMP, MPC, and URDFIL to solve displacement and phase-field equations in a staggered manner.
Enforce phase-field bounds and irreversibility through a primal-dual active-set approach.
infographic.evidence_signal: The implementation is demonstrated on silicate glass using the “Nine Circles of Elastic Brittle Fracture” tests, with deployment illustrated for native Abaqus elements including CPS3, CAX3, and C3D4.
infographic.watch_item: The presented formulation targets isotropic linear-elastic brittle materials; broader material behavior is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Abaqus implementation of the phase-field approach to fracture

title: A hybrid wave-mode formulation for the vibro-acoustic analysis of 2D periodic structures
authors: C. Droz, C. Zhou, M. N. N Ichchou, J. -P. Lain{é}
abstract: In the framework of vibrational analysis of 2D periodic waveguides, Floquet-Bloch theorem is widely applied for the determination of wave dispersion characteristics. In this context, the Wave Finite Element Method (WFEM) combines Periodic Structure Theory (PST) with standard FE packages, enabling wave dispersion analysis of waveguides involving structurally realistic unit-cells. For such applications, the computational efficiency of the WFEM, depends on the choice of the formulation and can lead to numerical issues, worsened by extensive computational cost. This paper presents a coupled wave-mode approach for the determination of wave dispersion characteristics in structurally advanced periodic structures. It combines two scales of model order reduction. At the unit-cell's scale, Component Mode Synthesis (CMS) provides the displacement field associated with local resonances of the periodic structure, while the free wave propagation is considered using a spectral problem projection on a reduced set of shape functions associated with propagating waves, thus providing considerable reduction of the computational cost. An application is provided for a bi-directionally stiffened panel and the influence of reduction parameters is discussed, as well as the robustness of the numerical results.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid wave-mode formulation reduces wave-dispersion computation in 2D periodic structures by combining unit-cell modal reduction with a reduced wave-propagation basis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports efficient vibration analysis of structurally realistic periodic panels using standard finite-element models.
method: Use component mode synthesis to represent unit-cell dynamics and local resonances.
Project the wave-propagation spectral problem onto a reduced set of propagating-wave shape functions.
Combine both reductions within a wave finite element framework.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an application to a bidirectionally stiffened panel, examining reduction parameters and numerical robustness, but provides no quantitative error or speedup figures.
infographic.watch_item: Reduced-basis selection requires care to preserve relevant local resonances and propagating waves.
infographic.paper_title: A hybrid wave-mode formulation for the vibro-acoustic analysis of 2D periodic structures

title: Vibro-acoustic optimisation of sandwich panels using the wave/finite element method
authors: C. Droz, Z. Zergoune, R. Boukadia, O. Bareille, M. N. N Ichchou
abstract: This paper investigates the use of a wave-based method in the framework of structural optimisation of composite panels involving advanced components. The wave/finite element method (WFEM) is used to evaluate the influence of a core's geometry on the transition frequency of a sandwich panel involving composite skins. This transition occurs is a sandwich panel when the transverse shear stiffness has a significant influence on the flexural motion, compared to the bending stiffness. It follows that the modal density and the acoustic radiation will considerably increase above this frequency. The periodic waveguide is modelled at the mesoscopic scale using a 3D finite element model of the unit-cell. Therefore this method does not require an homogenisation of the core based on Gibson and Ashby formulations to provide the wave dispersion characteristics. Although the cellular cores compared in this study share the same mass-to-stiffness ratio, a significant alteration of the transition frequency and modal density can be observed compared to honeycomb cores. A periodic octagonal core is designed, providing up to 70 % increase of the transition frequency and a significant reduction of the modal density.

infographic.key_insight: An octagonal sandwich-panel core raises the transition frequency by up to 70% and reduces modal density relative to honeycomb cores.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Core geometry can delay the onset of shear-influenced flexural motion associated with increased modal density and acoustic radiation.
method: Model a periodic unit cell with mesoscopic 3D finite elements.
Use the wave/finite element method to obtain dispersion characteristics without core homogenisation.
Compare core geometries through transition frequency and modal density.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparisons of cellular cores sharing the same mass-to-stiffness ratio, with the octagonal design achieving up to a 70% transition-frequency increase.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report experimental validation or quantify acoustic-radiation reductions.
infographic.paper_title: Vibro-acoustic optimisation of sandwich panels using the wave/finite element method

title: SLIM: Learning an Operator for Material-Efficient 3D Lattice Refinement
authors: Yueze Zhu, Yu Xing, Tianyang Xue, Peng-Shuai Wang, Jikai Liu, Haisen Zhao
abstract: Lattice inverse-design methods can generate cells that match prescribed effective properties, but property feasibility does not imply material efficiency. Removing redundant material from an existing lattice while preserving its homogenized elasticity ordinarily requires solving a separate constrained topology optimization problem for each cell, making large-scale refinement computationally expensive. We introduce SLIM (Structural Lightweighting via Implicit Mapping), a neural lattice-refinement model that replaces this per-instance iterative optimization with a single forward prediction. SLIM uses a dual-octree implicit network to predict the signed-distance field of a lightweight lattice and is trained on input--output pairs generated by property-constrained topology optimization. To improve stiffness preservation, we use homogenization sensitivities computed on the optimized target to estimate how residual voxel errors in a prediction affect its homogenized stiffness, and penalize this estimated change during training. Once trained, SLIM requires no topology optimization, homogenization analysis, or sensitivity evaluation during prediction. On the held-out test set of 906 lattices, SLIM achieves a mean relative volume-fraction reduction of 15.90%, a lightweighting success rate of 90.51%, and a mean normalized aggregate TO-target error of 0.636%, while reducing the average per-lattice generation time from 2516.0 s with direct TO to approximately 0.5 s. These results show that SLIM provides a fast neural surrogate for repeated topology-optimization-based refinement of 3D lattices.

infographic.key_insight: SLIM learns to remove redundant material from 3D lattices in a single forward prediction while approximately preserving homogenized elasticity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model enables rapid refinement of existing lattice designs without running topology optimization or homogenization analysis for each prediction.
method: Train a dual-octree implicit network to predict lightweight lattice signed-distance fields.
Use training pairs generated by property-constrained topology optimization.
Penalize estimated stiffness changes using target-based homogenization sensitivities.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 906 held-out lattices, SLIM achieved 15.90% mean relative volume-fraction reduction, 90.51% lightweighting success, and 0.636% mean normalized aggregate TO-target error, with generation taking approximately 0.5 s versus 2516.0 s for direct topology optimization.
infographic.watch_item: Training requires optimized targets and homogenization sensitivities; performance beyond the evaluated lattice distribution remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: SLIM: Learning an Operator for Material-Efficient 3D Lattice Refinement

title: Nondimensionalization, Variational Inequalities and Uncertainty Quantification in a Morphoelastic Model for Burn Injury Healing
authors: Wilbert den Hertog, Fred Vermolen
abstract: Mathematical modelling of burn injury healing involves coupling biological processes with mechanical deformation, resulting in computationally stiff, nonlinear partial differential equations that severely limit the scalability of existing numerical solutions. We present a computational framework addressing these challenges. By nondimensionalizing the model and performing scaling analysis, we show that chemotaxis and inertia are negligible, permitting a quasi-static momentum approach. To enforce non-negativity constraints, we implement a Variational Inequality formulation using the Finite Element Method in FEniCSx, and verify it via numerical convergence studies and mass balances. We identify high-order parameter interactions, specifically equilibrium collagen density and signalling dynamics, as the primary drivers of solver stability. A sensitivity analysis of nearly four million simulations reveals that isolated parameter variations predominantly govern the maximum wound contraction. In contrast, higher-order interactions determine the timing of maximum contraction and the permanent contracture. However, no significant pairwise parameter interactions were found, suggesting that the model's behaviour is governed by higher-order interactions, highlighting the inherent complexity of the wound-healing process.

infographic.key_insight: Maximum wound contraction is driven mainly by individual parameter variations, while its timing and permanent contracture depend on higher-order interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework simplifies coupled burn-healing mechanics and helps identify parameters critical to predicting contraction and maintaining solver stability.
method: Nondimensionalization and scaling analysis justify neglecting chemotaxis and inertia.
A FEniCSx finite element variational inequality formulation enforces non-negativity.
Large-scale sensitivity analysis quantifies individual and interacting parameter effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The formulation was verified through numerical convergence studies and mass balances, and sensitivity analysis covered nearly four million simulations.
infographic.watch_item: Solver stability is sensitive to higher-order parameter interactions, and the abstract reports numerical verification rather than clinical validation.
infographic.paper_title: Nondimensionalization, Variational Inequalities and Uncertainty Quantification in a Morphoelastic Model for Burn Injury Healing

title: Topology optimization of shipboard components for Navy shock certification via the Dynamic Design Analysis Method
authors: Miguel A. Aguilo
abstract: Shipboard equipment must survive the transient loads of underwater explosions. The U.S. Navy certifies such equipment with the Dynamic Design Analysis Method (DDAM), a modal response analysis driven by Navy shock design spectra. DDAM is well established as a verification tool, yet it is rarely used as a design driver in topology optimization. The design spectrum depends on the modal mass, a non-smooth coupling that classical sensitivity formulations do not address. This paper presents a complete differentiable formulation of the DDAM criterion for gradient-based topology optimization. Eigenvalue sensitivities follow the Fox-Kapoor method, and eigenvector sensitivities follow Nelson's method. The chain rule covers a spectral displacement that depends on both the natural frequency and the modal participation factor. Automatic differentiation assembles the sensitivity, and the engineer can certify components inside the optimization loop rather than after design. Three certification problems on a representative shipboard equipment frame demonstrate the workflow. In each, the optimizer removes 43.2% to 46.1% of the design-domain material and holds the certifying NRL Sum within 0.41% of the Navy allowable. Two companion studies follow. A compliance-optimized frame of nearly the same mass has a 5.2 Hz fundamental, outside the range the certification can qualify. Its nominal response also exceeds the allowable by a factor of 2.75. A lower bound on the mean of the two lowest eigenvalues separates the repeated pair that the demonstrations drive onto the frequency floor. The response then stops oscillating across the acceptance boundary. It ends at most 0.5% above the allowable, at a cost of under two percentage points of volume fraction.

infographic.key_insight: A differentiable DDAM formulation enables topology optimization to use Navy shock-certification criteria directly as design constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designing for shock response inside the optimization loop can reduce shipboard component material while avoiding layouts that perform well in compliance but fail certification criteria.
method: Differentiate DDAM spectral displacement through natural frequency and modal participation.
Use Fox–Kapoor eigenvalue sensitivities, Nelson eigenvector sensitivities, and automatic differentiation.
Constrain the mean of the two lowest eigenvalues to stabilize response near the frequency floor.
infographic.evidence_signal: Three equipment-frame certification problems removed 43.2–46.1% of design-domain material while keeping the certifying NRL Sum within 0.41% of the Navy allowable.
infographic.watch_item: Repeated low-frequency modes can cause acceptance-boundary oscillations; the added eigenvalue constraint stabilized the response but still ended up to 0.5% above the allowable.
infographic.paper_title: Topology optimization of shipboard components for Navy shock certification via the Dynamic Design Analysis Method

title: Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
authors: Yuanyu He, Zhuokun Chen, Yefei He, Zhiwei Tang, Jiasheng Tang, Yinghao Yu
abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.

infographic.key_insight: Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA) exploits localized motion to reduce redundant storage and computation in autoregressive video diffusion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: DASA could lower the cost of long-video generation, but its suitability for mechanics simulations or physically accurate motion is not established.
method: Separate dynamic and static regions using video-codec-inspired principles.
Compress historical KV caches by retaining dynamic features and allocate computation according to regional motion.
Use lightweight dynamics-guided distillation to preserve generation quality.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 2.16× faster autoregressive video generation with high visual fidelity in VBench evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Motion-based sparsification may require careful validation to avoid losing subtle dynamics or important static detail.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion

title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology
authors: Imanol García de Beristain, David Nieto Simavilla, Marco Ellero
abstract: We present GINNGER (GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for GEnerative Rheology), a framework for discovering thermodynamically admissible constitutive equations from microstructural flow data. Unlike existing approaches that learn constitutive operators, GINNGER reformulates constitutive discovery as the learning of the underlying thermodynamic generators from which constitutive equations emerge. Embedding the GENERIC formalism into the learning process restricts the search to constitutive models that satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction, eliminating the need to prescribe phenomenological constitutive equations a priori. A second conceptual advance is a spectral formulation of constitutive discovery in the intrinsic eigenspace of the polymer conformation tensor. This provides a kinematics-independent thermodynamic state space in which the thermodynamic generators depend only on the instantaneous microstructural state, while flow kinematics acts solely as an external driver transporting the system through this space. Consequently, data from shear, extensional, and mixed flows contribute to the discovery of a single constitutive model that generalizes across deformation protocols and flow geometries. By learning thermodynamic generators rather than high-dimensional constitutive operators, GINNGER substantially reduces the complexity of the discovery problem while preserving thermodynamic consistency, material objectivity, and physical interpretability by construction. The framework is validated using high-fidelity simulations, accurately reconstructing constitutive behavior and predicting complex flow fields across previously unseen geometries. GINNGER establishes a new paradigm for constitutive discovery by combining generative, spectral, and thermodynamically grounded learning within a unified framework for data-driven modeling of complex fluids.

infographic.key_insight: GINNGER learns thermodynamic generators rather than constitutive operators, yielding complex-fluid models that obey the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports transferable constitutive modeling of polymeric fluids across deformation protocols and flow geometries without prescribing phenomenological equations.
method: Embed GENERIC thermodynamic structure into neural-network learning.
Represent microstructural states in the polymer conformation tensor’s intrinsic eigenspace.
Combine shear, extensional, and mixed-flow data to discover one constitutive model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation with high-fidelity simulations, accurate constitutive reconstruction, and prediction of complex flow fields in previously unseen geometries.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation and quantitative accuracy are not reported in the abstract, leaving real-world robustness to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology

title: Mixed Unfitted finite element approximation of band structures in photonic crystals
authors: Yuyan Zou, Luke G. Bennetts, Hailong Guo
abstract: Photonic crystals are periodic dielectric structures whose optical properties are characterized by Maxwell eigenvalue problems with discontinuous material coefficients. For arbitrarily shaped inclusions, their numerical solution remains challenging due to costly mesh generation and remeshing as the geometry changes. In this paper, we address this challenge by developing a mixed unfitted finite element method based on the Floquet-Bloch transform. Our method uses a uniform background mesh independent of the inclusion geometry, thereby avoiding interface-fitted meshing and allowing us to impose the periodic boundary condition through a direct identification of degrees of freedom. A key feature of our construction is that the resulting finite element pairs preserve the de Rham commuting relation for the shifted operator. This structure enables us to establish an inf-sup condition uniformly with respect to the cut position and, in particular, to rule out spurious modes. We further establish optimal convergence of the eigenvalues and eigenspaces, with constants independent of both the mesh size and the position of the interface. Finally, we present extensive numerical experiments in two and three dimensions to validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the robustness of the proposed method.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed unfitted finite element method computes photonic-crystal band structures on geometry-independent meshes while preserving the shifted de Rham structure to exclude spurious modes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach avoids interface-fitted meshing and remeshing when inclusion shapes change, supporting photonic-crystal design studies.
method: Apply the Floquet–Bloch transform to the Maxwell eigenvalue problem.
Use a uniform background mesh and enforce periodicity by directly identifying degrees of freedom.
Construct compatible mixed finite element pairs with cut-position-independent inf-sup stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal eigenvalue and eigenspace convergence with mesh- and interface-position-independent constants, supported by extensive 2D and 3D numerical experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation must preserve the shifted commuting structure and correctly handle cut interfaces; the abstract provides no runtime or scalability benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Mixed Unfitted finite element approximation of band structures in photonic crystals
